messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Before the assault, Marcus had spent twenty-three years as a social worker in a community mental health clinic in Cleveland, a job that required him to enter homes, sit in cramped apartments, and listen to stories that others could not bear to hear. He was known for his steady presence, for the way he could sit with a client in a tiny, windowless intake room and make that space feel safe. That changed on a Tuesday evening in late October, when a client he had been seeing for six months attacked him in that same intake room. The man had been discharged from a residential program against Marcus’s recommendation, and during what Marcus had believed was a routine check-in, the client locked the door, pinned him against the wall, and sexually assaulted him. Marcus did not scream. He could not. He remembered the pressure of the man’s forearm against his throat, the smell of stale coffee and sweat, and the sound of the lock clicking into place—a sound he now heard in his mind dozens of times a day.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found that he could not stay in the office. The intake room was repainted and reassigned, but every time he walked past it, his chest tightened and his palms went cold. He began taking his lunch breaks outside, even in November rain, because the staff break room felt like a coffin. At home, his wife noticed that he would not enter the basement to do laundry unless she came with him, and he had stopped using the walk-in closet in their bedroom. He told her it was because the shelves were disorganized, but the truth was that the moment the door swung shut behind him, the air went thick and the walls seemed to tilt inward. He had come to believe that any enclosed space could become the trap he had not seen coming.

Marcus also began to check behind him. It was not a conscious decision at first—a glance over his shoulder while walking to his car, a quick scan of the parking lot before unlocking the door—but within a month it had become a compulsion that governed his movements. He would turn his head so often during his commute that his neck ached by the time he arrived home. He avoided unfamiliar places entirely. When his supervisor suggested he transfer to a different clinic across town, Marcus refused without explanation. He was certain that any new environment would hide dangers he could not anticipate. Even familiar routes felt unsafe if a detour forced him onto a street he did not know. When his wife was twenty minutes late coming home from the grocery store, Marcus stood at the front window, phone in hand, convinced that the delay meant something terrible had happened—that someone had followed her, that she had been attacked, that the world had once again revealed itself to be a place where violence arrived without warning.

He tried to push the memories away. When the image of the lock clicking into place surfaced during a staff meeting, he would force his mind to go blank, clenching his jaw until the thought dissolved. But the effort exhausted him, and the memories always returned, often at night, bringing with them the same suffocating terror he had felt in that room. What frightened him most, however, was not the fear but the shame. When he remembered the assault, he felt a hot, crawling shame that made him want to hide his face. He had been a social worker for two decades. He should have seen it coming. He should have been stronger. He could not find the words to describe what had happened, even to his wife. He knew the facts—he could list them in his clinical notes—but when he tried to speak aloud, the sentences dissolved into silence. His mouth went dry, and the memory of the forearm against his throat returned, and he could not say anything at all.

In the privacy of his own mind, Marcus spent hours ruminating about revenge. He imagined confronting the man in a parking lot, imagined the satisfaction of making him feel the same helplessness. He knew these thoughts were unproductive, even dangerous, but they gave him a strange sense of control. The fantasies were the only time he felt powerful rather than trapped.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a simple, practical failure. He had been assigned a new client—a young woman who had been assaulted in her own apartment—and he was supposed to meet her at a domestic violence shelter across town. The shelter was in a building he had never visited, in a neighborhood he did not know. He spent an hour driving in circles, pulling over three times to check his GPS, each delay feeding the certainty that something was about to go wrong. He never made it to the appointment. He called in sick, sat in his car in a grocery store parking lot, and wept. That evening, he told his wife that he needed help. He did not know if he could get better, but he knew he could not keep living this way—trapped in a world that had shrunk to the size of a single locked room.
